name: Defensive attribution hypothesis
statement: Observers blame the person behind an accident more as its consequences worsen, and blame that person less when they see themselves as similar to him.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and they pull in opposite directions. The first is Elaine Walster's: an accident that could have happened to anyone is frightening, so the worse the outcome, the more an observer wants somebody to have caused it. Blame rises with severity. The second is Kelly Shaver's amendment. An observer who resembles the person who caused the accident, and who might plausibly be in that position one day, has a competing motive, because blaming a person like oneself invites blame for one's own future mistakes. Such an observer should assign less responsibility as severity rises, not more. The hypothesis therefore predicts a main effect for one kind of observer and its reverse for another, and the two predictions were not made at the same time. Shaver proposed the second after the first failed to repeat.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Walster's paper is "Assignment of responsibility for an accident" and does not use the phrase defensive attribution. The name comes from the title of Shaver's 1970 paper in the same journal, which added the similarity variables after failing to repeat Walster's severity effect. Burger's 1981 review describes the joint position of the two papers as what became known as the defensive-attribution hypothesis.

evidence: Walster played 88 introductory psychology students, 44 women and 44 men, a tape of neighbours and teachers describing a young man called Lennie whose parked car rolled down a hill in Duluth after a rusted brake cable broke. Lennie's behaviour was identical on all four tapes. Only the outcome changed: a dented bumper, a wrecked car, or a car through a shop window that hurt a child and put the grocer in hospital for a year. Students rated responsibility on a four-point scale. Means were 2.5 and 3.0 where Lennie alone suffered, and 2.6 and 3.2 where others could suffer, F(1, 84) = 8.73, p < .01. The mechanism mattered as much as the result. Ratings of Lennie's carelessness did not move, F(1, 84) = 1.06, so students were not reinterpreting what he did. What moved was the standard they applied. Asked how often a person is morally obliged to have the brakes checked, students in the mild conditions said every 11.3 and 7.8 months and those in the severe conditions said every 9.0 and 7.1 months. A combined strictness index rose with severity, F(1, 68) = 5.62, p < .05. Walster also reported that sex of student interacted with severity where bystanders were at risk, F(1, 40) = 4.25, p < .05. Men rated Lennie 3.4 when he hit the grocer and 2.3 when he nearly did. Women rated him 3.0 either way.

replication.headline: Across 22 experiments the severity effect averaged d = 0.27, and dropping the single strongest study takes it to 0.09.
replication.detail: Jerry Burger collected 22 experiments from 21 articles that manipulated accident severity and measured responsibility assigned to the person who caused it. Six reported a positive relation, 15 found none, and one found a slight negative relation. Burger used Cooper's method of combining reported p levels, inserting p = .50 wherever a result was described as nonsignificant without a figure. The combined z was 3.165 unweighted, p < .001, and 3.943 weighted by sample size, p < .00005, with a fail-safe number of 59.4. The average d index across the 22 studies was 0.27, and the average U3 index of 61 means the typical severe-condition participant blamed the perpetrator more than 61% of mild-condition participants did. Burger then reported what that average rests on. Removing one study, Phares and Wilson's 1972 experiment, drops the average d to 0.09. Replacing its effect with the mean of the other five supportive studies, 0.50, still leaves 0.11. The similarity half fared better in his reading. Of the studies that measured personal or situational similarity, Burger counted all but one as supporting Shaver, including Chaikin and Darley's finding that people expecting to become supervisors blamed a supervisor less than people expecting to become workers did. Three of the four experiments using involving procedures supported the hypothesis, against eight of the 18 that used written vignettes alone. Burger's conclusion was that the evidence supports the hypothesis once similarity is taken into account, and that the bare severity effect is weak.

study.cite: Burger, J. M. (1981). Motivational biases in the attribution of responsibility for an accident: A meta-analysis of the defensive-attribution hypothesis. Psychological Bulletin, 90(3), 496-512.

limits: The d of 0.64 for Walster's own study is Burger's estimate, reconstructed from her reported p level and sample size, and it does not appear in her paper. Burger's method is a combination of p levels rather than of effect sizes, it treats every unreported null as p = .50, and it produces no confidence interval, so the pooled figures here carry none. Walster's 1967 follow-up was read in full from a scan on her own site, and is reported here from the paper rather than from Burger. One thing that reading changes is the direction: Burger's summary of it reads as a null, and the paper reports a significant reversal in its first experiment. That experiment was the one Burger could not enter in his table, because gains and losses were not reported separately, so the reversal is absent from every pooled figure above. Shaver's 1970 experiments were not obtained. Ovid marks the full text as paid, and the publisher's own record answered a bot challenge on 21 September 2026, so what Shaver found is reported here as Burger reports it, with the abstract read from Ovid. The same holds for the individual studies in Burger's table. Robbennolt published a later meta-analysis of outcome severity and responsibility judgements in 2000, whose abstract says the direction holds across methods while the strength varies by the judgement asked for. Its estimates were not retrieved, so no figure from it appears here. The severity manipulation is confounded with how likely the outcome seems, a point Burger discusses at length and does not resolve. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, the Open Science Framework registries and the open web on 21 September 2026 found no preregistered or multi-laboratory repeat of Walster's 1966 procedure. They did find a preregistration of a replication and extension of Shaver's second experiment, registered on the Open Science Framework in April 2024. No published report of it was found. Later work using the name tests something adjacent rather than the 1966 design: Salminen interviewed victims, co-workers and foremen after 99 serious occupational accidents in Finland. Pinciotti and Orcutt modelled whether blaming a rape victim lowers a person's own sense of vulnerability, which it did among 618 undergraduates for women and not for men.
misreadings: The version that circulates is the severity half on its own, which is the half that held up worst. Walster's own next study did not merely fail to find it. She described a house purchase whose outcome was a large, moderate or small gain or loss. Among 153 high-school juniors the effect ran backwards, and less responsibility was assigned as the consequences grew, F(1, 123) = 8.27, p < .01. Her second experiment found no trend of any shape. Walster called the failure to repeat disturbing and wrote that she could not explain it. Shaver then failed to find it too, which is why the similarity variables exist at all. Readers also take the hypothesis to predict more victim blaming among people who feel at risk. It predicts the opposite for observers who could see themselves in the position of causing the harm, and the mechanism runs through blame avoidance rather than through indifference. Burger's headline verdict is often quoted as support for the hypothesis without the sentence that follows it, where he shows the pooled effect falling to 0.09 when one study is removed. Walster's data are also read as showing that people rewrite what the careless person did. Her carelessness ratings did not shift. Only the moral standard shifted. The idea is close enough to the just-world hypothesis that Burger, following Chaikin and Darley, judged the two to spring from the same assumptions and doubted that a situation could be designed where they predict different things.

sources.text: Walster, E. (1966). Assignment of responsibility for an accident. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 3(1), 73-79. Source for the design, the condition means, the F tests and the sex interaction. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from a copy hosted at elainehatfield.com, and every figure above was checked against it.

Walster, E. (1967). 'Second guessing' important events. Human Relations, 20(3), 239-249. Walster's own follow-up, whose first experiment found a significant reversal of the severity effect. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from a scan at elainehatfield.com, the site this entry already uses for her 1966 paper. The scan carries no text layer and was read by optical character recognition, so the two F values quoted from it were re-read at higher resolution to confirm the digits.

Shaver, K. G. (1970). Defensive attribution: Effects of severity and relevance on the responsibility assigned for an accident. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 14(2), 101-113. The paper the name comes from. Not obtained on 21 September 2026. Ovid marks the full text as paid, and the publisher's record answered a bot challenge rather than a paywall. The abstract was read from Ovid; the rest is described here as Burger describes it.

Burger, J. M. (1981). Motivational biases in the attribution of responsibility for an accident: A meta-analysis of the defensive-attribution hypothesis. Psychological Bulletin, 90(3), 496-512. Source for every pooled figure quoted. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from an archived copy of the Santa Clara University PDF, since the live copy now returns a 404.

Phares, E. J., & Wilson, K. G. (1972). Responsibility attribution: Role of outcome severity, situational ambiguity, and internal-external control. Journal of Personality, 40(3), 392-406. The study whose removal takes Burger's average d from 0.27 to 0.09. Not obtained; Wiley answered a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026. Its result is quoted here from Burger.

Chaikin, A. L., & Darley, J. M. (1973). Victim or perpetrator?: Defensive attribution of responsibility and the need for order and justice. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 25(2), 268-275. Not obtained; the publisher's record answered a bot challenge on 21 September 2026. Its results are quoted here from Burger.

Robbennolt, J. K. (2000). Outcome severity and judgments of 'responsibility': A meta-analytic review. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 30(12), 2575-2609. Abstract read from the Crossref record on 21 September 2026; its estimates were not retrieved for this entry.

Salminen, S. (1992). Defensive attribution hypothesis and serious occupational accidents. Psychological Reports, 70(3, Pt 2), 1195-1199. Abstract read from the Crossref record on 21 September 2026, for the design and the direction of the result.

Pinciotti, C. M., & Orcutt, H. K. (2020). It won't happen to me: An examination of the effectiveness of defensive attribution in rape victim blaming. Violence Against Women, 26(10), 1059-1079. Abstract read from the Crossref record on 21 September 2026, for the sample and the pattern by sex.
